newsitem.title: BURMA: Suu Kyi public meetings likely after barriers go.
newsitem.headline: Suu Kyi public meetings likely after barriers go.

text.p: Burmese opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi responded to the military's removal of checkpoints barring access to her house on Tuesday by saying she was ready to resume her recently aborted weekly public gatherings.

"A few blockades do not constitute obstacles to democratisation. We shall have to meet as long as people desire to meet. Come and see," Suu Kyi told a news conference hours after the checkpoints were removed when asked if she would hold her weekly public meetings again.
The checkpoints were set up on September 26 to prevent Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) from holding a party congress from September 27-29.
But they also stopped her from holding her public gatherings for two straight weekends. The gatherings outside her University Avenue home had been attended by thousands of her supporters.
The ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) also detained 573 NLD members and supporters in a subsequent crackdown. All but 63 have since been released.
"What the SLORC did during the past 10 days did not damage the NLD. But they were illegal processes that damaged the reputation of the SLORC," said a relaxed Suu Kyi.

But the Nobel laureate remained hopeful of dialogue with the SLORC, something that has not transpired since the NLD last November pulled out of a National Convention set up to draw a new constitution for Burma.
The NLD withdrawal angered the SLORC and the two sides have been on a collision course since then.
On the possibility of whether a dialogue could start between the SLORC and the NLD, Suu Kyi, who was released from six years of house arrest last year, said that was her ultimate goal.
"I have always said that in the end we will get to the dialogue," she added.

When asked if she supported a recent U.S. ban on travel visas for some senior Burmese leaders and their families to the United States, she said: "We support all actions that are intended to help in democractisation."

U.S. President Bill Clinton imposed the travel ban after the Burmese military prevented the NLD congress and detained the party's activists. The SLORC responded by restricting its visas for certain categories of American citizens.

Suu Kyi also said that the NLD also wanted to re-open its downtown headquarters and its offices in various townships that were closed by the SLORC on September 28 after the crackdown on party activists.

"It (the headquarters) was closed down because of illegal action," she said. The headquarters office would be re-opened at the same place where it was before, she said without giving a time frame for the action.
